analysis.one_liner: Shields drug, vaccine, and device makers from lawsuits over pandemic and bioterror products.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate health committee: it was referred on the day it was introduced, drew zero cosponsors, and died when the Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have rewritten the rules for anyone harmed by a drug, vaccine, or device used against a pandemic, epidemic, or bioterror attack. Instead of suing the manufacturer or the hospital that gave the shot, an injured person could only sue the U.S. government in one federal court in Washington, D.C., under a process that starts from the assumption the government cannot be held liable [S2][S3]. To lift that shield, the Health and Human Services Secretary would have to find clear and convincing evidence that the company willfully broke the law in a way that caused a significant health risk and the specific injury — and the Secretary's decision whether to even investigate could not be challenged in court [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Manufacturers, distributors, and health care providers of pandemic, epidemic, and bioterror countermeasures would gain near-total protection from lawsuits, no matter how a product was designed, made, labeled, or administered — including products sold to private customers, not just the government [S3]. Taxpayers would pick up the bill instead, since claims would be redirected to the U.S. Treasury through the federal courts.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Drug, vaccine, and bioterror product makers

how_it_helps.text: The bill replaces all lawsuits against manufacturers, distributors, and health care providers with a single federal claim against the United States, heard only in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia [S2][S3].

The federal government would enjoy a rebuttable presumption of immunity covering claims about products drawn from the National Strategic Stockpile, products procured by the HHS Secretary, and any product designated during an actual or potential public health emergency — and the protection would apply to products sold to private customers as well as the government [S2][S3].

The only way to defeat the immunity presumption is for the Secretary to find, by clear and convincing evidence, that a company intentionally or with willful disregard violated federal drug law in a way that created a significant health risk and caused the injury — a very high bar — and manufacturers get a formal hearing plus the right to appeal any adverse finding, which automatically suspends it while the case is reviewed [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: People injured or killed by a qualified pandemic product or bioterror countermeasure would lose their day in court against the company or provider that made or administered the product. Their only path would be suing the U.S. government, where the government starts with a presumption of immunity and the Secretary can decline to investigate a complaint without ever having to explain that choice to a judge [S2][S3]. Taxpayers would bear the cost of any compensation instead of the manufacturers.
analysis.who_pays_short: People injured by these products, and taxpayers

drawbacks.text: An injured person's only remedy would be a federal claim against the United States that begins with a presumption of immunity, in a single courthouse, and the Secretary's refusal to investigate a claim cannot be reviewed by any court [S2][S3].

Even if the Secretary did find willful misconduct, the manufacturer could appeal and the filing of that appeal automatically suspends the determination while the case proceeds — and injured people would be barred from joining that appeal as parties, with no subpoenas or compulsory process allowed [S3].

The good-faith case for liability shields is that fear of lawsuits keeps companies from making vaccines and antidotes for rare threats, which could leave the country without critical supplies in a real emergency; the honest cost of this bill is that it removed any meaningful consequence for a company whose product harms people, with the burden shifted to the injured person and the taxpayer.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Whatever the supply-side argument for encouraging countermeasure development, this version of the idea was extremely one-sided: it would have wiped out liability for every stage of a product's life — design, testing, manufacturing, labeling, and administration — for products sold to ordinary customers, not just government stockpile purchases, and it placed the decision to investigate wrongdoing entirely in the discretion of an official whose refusal no court could question [S2][S3]. The protections for injured people were so narrow that the bill reads far more as a shield for industry than as a preparedness measure for the public.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate health committee the same day, the committee never took it up, and it died quietly when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Sen. Judd Gregg introduced the bill on July 20, 2005, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions that same day [S1][S5].
No further action was ever taken; the committee never held a hearing or a markup, and no vote was ever scheduled in the Senate or the House [S5].
No senator ever cosponsored the bill — the cosponsor count was zero for the life of the bill [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without any committee action, injured people kept the ordinary ability to sue a negligent manufacturer or provider under existing law, and drug and vaccine makers gained nothing from this bill. (It is widely known that Congress did enact similar liability protections for countermeasures later in 2005 through a different bill, the PREP Act — that is outside the record for this legislation.)

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Injured patients kept their right to sue

for.name: Sen. Judd Gregg
for.role: U.S. Senator from New Hampshire; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and sent it to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on the day of introduction.

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on July 20, 2005 and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote, leaving the bill to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no senator besides the sponsor was attached to the bill, so there was never a record of who supported or opposed it [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would have given them blanket immunity from lawsuits over pandemic and bioterror products at every stage from design to administration, including products sold to private customers [S3]. Their gain would come directly out of the legal rights of anyone their products injured.

industries.industry: Health care providers and distributors of countermeasures
industries.note: Hospitals, clinics, and volunteers administering countermeasures would be shielded from lawsuits, which supporters said would encourage participation in an emergency response; the cost is that a patient harmed by negligent administration could only pursue a federal claim against the U.S. government under a presumption of immunity [S2][S3].
All liability would shift from private companies to the United States itself, so taxpayers would fund compensation for injuries while the government holds a default presumption that it owes nothing.
